blocks.text: His face had a strong—a very strong—shape like an eagle’s. His thin nose had a high bridge, and his nostrils curved in an unusual way. His forehead was high and rounded. Little hair grew at the sides of his forehead, but it grew thickly everywhere else. His eyebrows were very thick and almost met above his nose. Their bushy hairs seemed to curl because there were so many of them. I could only see part of his mouth under his thick moustache. It was set firmly and looked rather cruel, with unusually sharp white teeth. These stuck out over his lips. His lips were so remarkably red that he seemed astonishingly full of life for a man of his age. His ears were pale, with extremely pointed tops. His chin was broad and strong, and his cheeks were firm but thin. Altogether, he looked extraordinarily pale.

Until then, I had noticed the backs of his hands resting on his knees in the firelight. They had seemed rather white and delicate. But now they were close to me, and I could not help noticing their rather rough appearance. They were broad, with short, thick fingers. Strangely, there were hairs in the centre of his palm. His nails were long and narrow, and cut to sharp points. As the Count leaned over me and his hands touched me, I could not stop myself shaking. Perhaps it was because his breath smelled so bad. But a horrible sick feeling came over me, and nothing I did could hide it. The Count clearly noticed it and drew back. He gave a rather hard smile, showing his teeth sticking out more clearly than before. Then he sat down again on his own side of the fireplace. We were both silent for a while. I looked towards the window and saw the first faint line of approaching daylight. Everything seemed strangely still. But as I listened, I heard many wolves howling. The sound seemed to come from down below in the valley. The Count’s eyes shone, and he said:—
“Listen to them—the children of the night. What music they make!” I suppose he saw an expression on my face that seemed strange to him. He added:—
“Ah, sir, you people who live in cities cannot understand a hunter’s feelings.” Then he stood up and said:—

“But you must be tired. Your bedroom is all ready. Tomorrow you shall sleep as late as you like. I have to be away until the afternoon. So sleep well and dream well!” He bowed politely and himself opened the door for me into the eight-sided room. I went into my bedroom....

I am lost in a sea of strange and wonderful things. I have doubts; I am afraid. I think strange things that I dare not even admit to my own soul. May God protect me, if only for the sake of those dear to me!

7 May.—It is early morning again. But I have rested and enjoyed the last twenty-four hours. I slept until late in the day and woke without anyone waking me. After I dressed, I went into the room where we had eaten supper. A cold breakfast was ready for me there. The coffee pot stood by the fire to keep the coffee hot. There was a card on the table with these words:—

“I have to be away for a while. Do not wait for me.—D.” I began eating and enjoyed a large meal. Afterwards, I looked for a bell to tell the servants I had finished. But I could not find one. Some things are certainly strangely missing from this house. This is surprising, because everything around me shows such great wealth. The things used to serve meals are made of gold. They are so beautifully made that they must be worth an enormous amount. The curtains, the cloth covering the chairs and sofas, and the curtains around my bed are all beautiful. They are made from the most expensive cloth. They must have been worth an extraordinary amount when they were made. They are hundreds of years old, yet still in excellent condition. I saw things like them in Hampton Court. But those were worn, with loose threads at the edges and holes eaten by moths. Yet there is no mirror in any of the rooms. There is not even a small mirror on my dressing table. I had to take my little shaving mirror from my bag before I could shave or brush my hair. I have not yet seen a servant anywhere. Nor have I heard any sound near the castle except wolves howling. Some time after my meal, I looked for something to read. I do not know whether to call the meal breakfast or dinner. It was between five and six o’clock when I ate it. I did not want to walk about the castle before asking the Count’s permission. There was absolutely nothing in the room to read: no book or newspaper. There were not even any writing materials. So I opened another door in the room and found a sort of library. I tried the door opposite mine, but it was locked.
